subtitle: Engaging cultural and ethnic communities starts with relationships. Learn to build connections that help communities shape decisions, while never treating any one person as a spokesperson for everyone.
scope: For leaders planning engagement with cultural and ethnic communities. The examples concern general relationship and service-design practices. Matters involving Native American communities or Tribal relations should be referred to the person or area responsible within ADSA.
introTranscript: Culture matters in relationships, but it is not a script that predicts what a person thinks. This course asks you to examine your assumptions, learn who is already doing community work, choose a meaningful question, arrange participation, and return with what changed. It uses a practice redesign of service information. You will practice working with community partners as knowledgeable colleagues and checking differences within a community, without reducing people to a language need or a disparity.

intro.heading: Begin with questions about your assumptions
intro.body:
A leader can prepare by learning context and still arrive with mistaken assumptions. Shared identity does not mean identical language, age, disability experience, migration history, or views about services. A community label cannot tell you how an individual prefers to communicate.

For a practice service-information redesign, “This group prefers family involvement” is an assumption unless people actually describe that preference. Ask who should be involved in the decision and provide choices. Some may welcome relatives; others may want privacy.

Write down what you think you know, how you know it, and what you need to ask. A respectful correction is useful evidence, not an embarrassment to defend against. Cultural humility includes changing your approach when the answer challenges the plan.

What is the best adjustment?
lessons.keyStatement: Use culture as a reason to ask better questions, not a shortcut to answers.

flashcards.back: A person or organization bringing knowledge and relationships; not automatically a representative of every member.
Variation in experiences, preferences, and circumstances among people sharing an identity.
A relationship in which participants can identify value, influence, and responsibilities on both sides.
Ongoing examination of assumptions and willingness to learn rather than claiming mastery of others.
A meaningful choice about whether, how, and what to contribute.

items.title: Assumption
items.body: An assumption can be useful as a question but harmful as a fact. In the leaflet case, a belief about family involvement should prompt an invitation to choose, not a rule requiring relatives at every discussion. Record its basis before acting on it.

items.title: Variation
items.body: People sharing an identity can differ in privacy, language, age, disability experience, and service use. Ask which experiences the current invitation misses. A different preference does not make someone less authentic or less worthy of consideration.

items.title: Correction
items.body: When a partner corrects the plan, examine the evidence before defending your preparation. Offering individual and family participation may preserve both preferences. The leader’s task is to revise the design, not to win an argument about the community.

tabs.label: Shortcut
tabs.body: One uniform support plan is administratively easy but may exclude people whose preferences differ. It also turns a community label into an individual prediction. Use background to prepare questions, then arrange feasible choices with participants.

tabs.label: Question
tabs.body: An open question makes room for an answer the team did not expect. Ask what would make participation workable, explain real limits, and avoid offering choices the team cannot deliver. This combines respect with operational honesty.

tabs.label: Reflection
tabs.body: Naming the original assumption is useful when it explains a changed practice, not as a performance of humility. Show how the invitation now allows different involvement preferences and check whether that change addressed the concern.

check.question: Which question avoids a cultural shortcut?
check.correct: Ask participants which involvement and communication options work for them.
wrong: Require a partner to explain every member.
check.feedbackCorrect: The question recognizes individual preference and within-community variation.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A family pattern, surname, or single partner’s view cannot establish everyone’s needs. Those shortcuts may feel knowledgeable but restrict choice without evidence. Ask about communication and involvement preferences and retain differences rather than requiring people to fit the original plan.

items.text: A label predicts everyone’s contact preference.
A leader infers needs from appearance.
A participant requests an individual call.
A partner describes who the invitation is missing.
Which options would make this usable?
Whose experience might differ?

options: Offer participation choices and revise the assumption.
Exclude the partner’s view as atypical.
responses: Background does not override individual preference.
This turns correction into a better engagement design.

intro.heading: Map relationships without appointing representatives
intro.body:
A trusted organization may know the issue well and still not reach every person affected. Begin by asking who already works on the concern, how relationships developed, and which experiences are missing. Do not choose a single partner because they are easiest for the agency to contact.

In the service-information case, an urban organization may hear from people who use online services, while rural residents and people without reliable internet are absent. That does not invalidate the organization. It identifies the need for additional routes.

Explain why you want a connection and avoid asking partners to provide names or private histories unnecessarily. Agree on an appropriate way to invite people. Relationship mapping is a planning tool, not a ranking of authenticity or a directory of sensitive personal data.

items.title: Existing work
items.body: Find out what organizations and informal networks already do before asking them to recruit participants. A service-navigation group may have valuable relationships and limited capacity. Explain the task and negotiate its role rather than assuming it will supply people on demand.

items.title: Coverage
items.body: A connection is evidence of a relationship, not comprehensive coverage. Ask which experiences reach the partner and which do not. If rural users are absent, add an appropriate route while retaining the useful urban relationship; incompleteness is not failure.

items.title: Invitation
items.body: Agree on how invitations will be shared. A partner can circulate a clear request without giving the agency a private list of service users. Ask only for information needed for the agreed purpose and avoid collecting sensitive histories to fill a participation map.

tabs.label: Convenient
tabs.body: Using one familiar contact saves time, but familiarity can hide missing experiences. Keep the relationship and examine its scope; do not turn ease of access into a claim that the entire community has been consulted.

tabs.label: Expanded
tabs.body: Additional routes may improve reach but also create burdens for partners and participants. Explain why the gap matters, coordinate efforts, and avoid repeated unconnected requests that make people carry the agency’s planning work.

tabs.label: Respectful
tabs.body: A negotiated invitation respects the partner’s capacity and relationships. The partner may decline a recruitment role or suggest a different method. That choice gives useful planning information rather than evidence of disloyalty.

check.question: What does one organization’s involvement establish?
check.correct: A useful relationship whose scope should be understood and supplemented where needed.
wrong: Permission to obtain private participant lists.
Proof that no further outreach is needed.
check.feedbackCorrect: Relationship and coverage are related but not interchangeable.
check.feedbackIncorrect: One organization can offer strong knowledge without representing every experience. Demanding private lists or treating a contact as complete coverage overstates its role. Keep the relationship, understand its scope, and develop additional appropriate routes for the missing perspectives.

items.text: A local group already provides service navigation.
An informal network offers to discuss the invitation.
Who is not reached by online outreach?
Which rural experiences are missing?
This organization speaks for all members.
One contact proves full engagement.

options: Keep the partnership and plan additional outreach to missing experiences.
Replace the organization for being incomplete.
responses: This values the relationship while addressing the gap.
No organization can be expected to cover every experience.

move.control: You can distinguish relationships from coverage.
move.failure: Convenient contacts become a false claim of broad participation.

lessons.title: Offer a purpose people can influence
lessons.summary: Write an invitation with an open question and clear limits.
lessons.objective: Write an invitation with an open question and clear limits.
objectives: Write an invitation with an open question and clear limits.
Identify the value and burden of participation from the partner’s perspective.
Distinguish consultation on a choice from promotion of a completed decision.
takeaways: Describe actual influence before asking for time.
Promise only confirmed arrangements and a real response.
lessons.statement: Do not invite influence that the process cannot deliver.

image.caption: Colleagues share information and consider a decision together.

intro.heading: Offer a purpose people can influence
intro.body:
People may have been asked repeatedly for input without seeing an answer. Explain what remains undecided, how the contribution will be used, who decides, and when the response will come. If a decision is fixed, describe the event honestly as information or implementation discussion.

A partner reviewing a service leaflet needs to know whether they can suggest a different contact route or only identify confusing wording. The task should fit the available influence and the time being requested. Ask what would make participation worthwhile, not just whether a calendar slot works.

Be clear about arrangements for time, access, and any compensation; do not promise payment before authority is confirmed. Matters involving Native American communities or Tribal relations should be referred to the person or area responsible within ADSA.

Identify the value and burden of participation from the partner’s perspective.
Distinguish consultation on a choice from promotion of a completed decision.
What is the honest response?
lessons.keyStatement: Do not invite influence that the process cannot deliver.

items.title: Purpose
items.body: State the choice that input can change. In the leaflet case, explain whether participants can alter contact routes, wording, or a later revision. A broad claim of shared design is misleading if the current document is already final.

items.title: Value
items.body: Ask what contribution is being requested and what it costs people in time or effort. Explain the value of participation from both perspectives. If partners need a usable summary or a response to an old question, include that need in planning.

items.title: Limits
items.body: Fixed decisions should be described as fixed, with the reason and appropriate questions still open. Do not promise universal adoption or unapproved payment to recruit people. Credibility comes from influence and arrangements the agency can actually deliver.

tabs.label: Promotion
tabs.body: Promotion can be legitimate when people are told the design is complete. Calling it engagement creates false expectations and can make a later invitation harder to trust. State the actual purpose rather than upgrading its label.

tabs.label: Engagement
tabs.body: An open choice allows participants to question assumptions and propose an alternative. It also creates responsibility for a response. The team must plan how it will explain adoption or refusal, not only how it will collect comments.

tabs.label: Information
tabs.body: Information about a fixed requirement can still invite useful implementation questions. Keep that distinction clear: explaining a rule is different from asking whether the group can change it. Route unresolved authority questions appropriately.

check.question: What makes an invitation credible?
check.correct: A real open question, accurate limits, participation arrangements, and a response date.
wrong: A promise to adopt every suggestion.
A request for agreement called shared design.
check.feedbackCorrect: Credibility depends on deliverable influence and dependable arrangements.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Promising every suggestion will be adopted may encourage attendance but is rarely deliverable. A finished design labeled shared design and unapproved payment also mislead people. A credible invitation states an open question, accurate limits, confirmed arrangements, and a response plan.

items.text: Compare two contact routes before selection.
Suggest clearer wording before release.
Explain an already authorized date.
Describe a rule the group cannot change.
Every suggestion will become policy.
Everyone will be paid before approval exists.

lessons.next: Next: Choose participation methods suited to different communication and access needs.

scenario.context: DHS practice case: A partner asks how input will matter. The leaflet is already printed, but the leader calls the event shared design.
options: Keep the label to encourage attendance.
Explain the fixed leaflet and identify any genuine implementation choices or a later redesign.
responses: Honest limits allow people to make an informed choice.
Such a promise exceeds the process.

lessons.transfer: Rewrite an invitation with influence, limits, burden, arrangements, and response date.

move.control: You can explain purpose and limits before asking for time.
move.failure: Participation feels like endorsement obtained under misleading terms.

lessons.summary: Choose participation methods suited to different communication and access needs.
lessons.objective: Choose participation methods suited to different communication and access needs.
objectives: Choose participation methods suited to different communication and access needs.
Identify barriers created by a single meeting format.
Revise a session plan with partner input and usable follow-up options.
takeaways: Match the repair to the actual participation barrier.
Coordinate qualified support and realistic options.
Check meaning before attributing conclusions to participants.
lessons.statement: Adapt the process with people rather than deciding their needs for them.

image.caption: Colleagues share information and consider a decision together.

intro.heading: Adapt participation with partners
intro.body:
A meeting method can make one person comfortable and leave another unable to contribute. Ask about language, communication, timing, disability access, transport, technology, and privacy as relevant. Do not infer those needs from ethnic identity.

For the leaflet review, offer a small discussion, a scheduled call, or written input where feasible. Arrange qualified language and accessibility support through the appropriate process. Translation of a document alone does not make a rushed technical discussion understandable.

Use a manageable question, explain terms, and allow time for interpretation and reflection. Check whether the summary matches what participants meant. A flexible process still needs a clear purpose and fair opportunities; it does not mean staff can skip applicable meeting or records requirements.

Identify barriers created by a single meeting format.
Revise a session plan with partner input and usable follow-up options.
What should the team do?
lessons.keyStatement: Adapt the process with people rather than deciding their needs for them.

items.title: Choice
items.body: Discuss realistic methods with participants rather than inferring preferences. A written route, scheduled call, or small session may meet different needs. Explain what each option permits and confirm resources so the choice is meaningful rather than decorative.

items.title: Support
items.body: Translation, interpretation, disability support, timing, and technology can be separate needs. If shift work blocks an evening meeting, translating the packet alone leaves the barrier intact. Coordinate qualified support and the appropriate process for each identified need.

items.title: Meaning
items.body: Check meaning after discussion, especially where technical language or interpretation is involved. A participant’s correction of the summary may reveal a design implication the team missed. Attendance or fluent delivery is not evidence that the intended message was understood.

tabs.label: Single route
tabs.body: One evening video route is easy to organize but can exclude schedules, connection limits, or communication needs. Absence cannot be interpreted as indifference until the participation conditions have been considered.

tabs.label: Adapted
tabs.body: An adapted plan can improve access and requires coordination. Discuss feasible times and methods with partners, retain the same decision question across routes, and be transparent when an option cannot be provided.

tabs.label: Verified
tabs.body: A corrected summary supports reliable interpretation of input. It may require revisiting a theme or recommendation, but that cost is preferable to confidently using a message participants did not mean.

check.question: What is the best response to a participation barrier?
check.correct: Ask about usable options and revise the method with appropriate support.
wrong: Assume a culture has one meeting preference.
Use a child to interpret a complex discussion.
Count attendance as proof of understanding.
check.feedbackCorrect: A usable process combines informed choices, support, and checks on meaning.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Translation can help and still leave schedule, technology, or privacy barriers unresolved. A child is not an appropriate substitute for qualified complex-discussion support, and attendance does not prove understanding. Ask about workable routes and check the meaning of the contribution.

items.text: Only a technical video meeting is offered.
Materials arrive too late for review.
Participants choose a feasible call option.
Qualified support is coordinated.
Participants correct the summary.
The facilitator asks what remained unclear.

options: Treat translation as the whole solution.
Discuss alternative times and methods alongside communication support.
Conclude that absent people were uninterested.
responses: Translation does not address schedule and technology barriers.
This matches the repair to the actual barriers.
Absence does not establish lack of interest.

move.control: You can adjust the method and verify meaning.
move.failure: An invitation exists but participation remains inaccessible.

lessons.title: Interpret input without flattening differences
lessons.summary: Separate participant statements from staff interpretations.
lessons.objective: Separate participant statements from staff interpretations.
objectives: Separate participant statements from staff interpretations.
Retain differences and limits when summarizing engagement.
Route identifying or formal concerns without losing the general design issue.
takeaways: Distinguish a statement from an interpretation.
Keep design-relevant differences in the summary.
State coverage and evidence limits without stereotyping.
lessons.statement: A summary should preserve meaning and uncertainty.

image.caption: Colleagues share information and consider a decision together.

intro.heading: Interpret input without flattening differences
intro.body:
Themes help a team use input, but they can erase important differences. Record what participants actually said and distinguish your interpretation. Do not describe a small group’s comments as what an entire community believes.

If one person wants family contact and another requests privacy, the useful theme may be contact choice. It is not proof that “the community wants families involved.” Ask participants to correct the account where feasible and report whose experiences the process did not reach.

Avoid placing identifying service histories in a public summary. Formal complaints, accommodation requests, or eligibility disputes need the responsible route. The design concern can be recorded without private identifiers. This preserves both meaningful input and appropriate authority.

inThisLesson: Separate participant statements from staff interpretations.
Retain differences and limits when summarizing engagement.
Route identifying or formal concerns without losing the general design issue.
What is the best revision?
lessons.keyStatement: A summary should preserve meaning and uncertainty.

items.title: Evidence
items.body: Keep the statement and the team’s interpretation separate. “I prefer a private call” is a participant’s contribution; “contact choice may improve access” is a staff proposal. That distinction allows others to inspect the reasoning without confusing an idea with a verified finding.

items.title: Difference
items.body: Retain differences that change the design. Family contact and individual privacy preferences can both support a choice-based approach. Removing the less convenient preference turns a theme into a stereotype and hides who the proposed design may exclude.

items.title: Boundary
items.body: An identifying service history does not need to appear in a public theme summary. Arrange formal complaints or disputes through their proper route while retaining a general question about clarity or access. Do not imply that a design theme resolves an individual case.

tabs.label: Overclaim
tabs.body: A universal community statement is concise but exceeds a small discussion’s evidence. Describe who participated, what was said, and who was missing. That precision supports useful learning without suggesting representative prevalence.

tabs.label: Accurate
tabs.body: An accurate account may include contradictory preferences and still be actionable. Explain the trade-off and test a flexible option rather than selecting the easier view and calling it consensus.

tabs.label: Useful
tabs.body: A choice-based design is a hypothesis to examine, not automatic proof of success. Explain that it follows from differing preferences, then check whether people can actually use the offered routes.

check.question: Which summary is sound?
check.correct: Participants expressed different contact preferences; the team will test a choice-based approach and note coverage limits.
wrong: The entire community prefers family contact.
All participants agree because disagreement was omitted.
Private case histories should be published to prove the theme.
check.feedbackCorrect: The account is specific, preserves difference, and avoids unsupported representation.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Claiming an entire community prefers family contact erases the conflicting privacy preference. Omitting dissent or publishing private histories may make a summary seem stronger while weakening accuracy and protection. Report the actual differences and the limits of the participants reached.

items.text: A participant requests a private call.
A participant asks to involve a relative.
The team proposes contact choice.
Staff believe the leaflet needs a clearer explanation.
Rural experiences were not reached.
The discussion does not establish prevalence.

scenario.context: DHS practice case: A draft says a whole community prefers family contact after two people offered conflicting preferences.
options: Report differing preferences and propose choice while noting the limited group.
Remove the private preference as inconvenient.
responses: The revision turns difference into a useful design question.
The omitted view may be central to access and privacy.

lessons.transfer: Revise one theme statement to separate evidence, interpretation, difference, and limit.

move.control: You can check summaries and avoid representation claims.
move.failure: People’s words become a stereotype in the decision record.

lessons.title: Keep the relationship after the event
lessons.summary: Prepare a response explaining what input changed and what remained unresolved.
lessons.objective: Prepare a response explaining what input changed and what remained unresolved.
objectives: Prepare a response explaining what input changed and what remained unresolved.

takeaways: Return with the decision and its reasons.
Repair missed arrangements through the people or areas responsible.
Respect participation choices and invite a review of usefulness.
lessons.statement: Trust depends on follow-through that people can see.

image.caption: Colleagues share information and consider a decision together.

intro.heading: Keep the relationship after the event
intro.body:
An engagement event is one moment in a relationship. Return with the decision, reasons, and outstanding questions in a usable form. If the team cannot adopt a suggestion, explain the actual reason rather than ending with a generic thank-you.

In the leaflet example, show the revised contact choices, identify unresolved usability concerns, and name the next review. If promised payment or access support was missed, address that directly with the person or area responsible; a positive report does not repair the missed commitment.

Ask whether the process was worth participants’ time and what should change next. Do not score partners by agreement with staff. A sustainable relationship allows criticism, boundaries, and the choice not to participate again.

Identify a missed engagement commitment and a proportionate repair.

lessons.keyStatement: Trust depends on follow-through that people can see.

items.title: Response
items.body: Show participants the decision and reasons in a usable form. For the leaflet, identify the new contact choices and any suggestion not adopted. A general thank-you does not allow people to judge whether their work influenced the result.

items.title: Repair
items.body: Address missed commitments directly. If support or a confirmed payment was delayed, involve the person or area responsible and give a named contact and update. A positive account of engagement cannot substitute for delivering what participants were promised.

items.title: Review
items.body: Ask about usefulness without measuring agreement or loyalty. A partner may decline another request after an unanswered contribution. Provide the overdue response and respect the boundary; continuing involvement should remain a choice rather than a proof of commitment.

tabs.label: Event count
tabs.body: Attendance totals can describe activity but not whether a relationship was reciprocal. Combine them with evidence of the response, delivery of arrangements, and participants’ opportunity to correct the interpretation.

tabs.label: Follow-through
tabs.body: A traceable response can strengthen trust even when some advice was not adopted. Explain actual reasons and unresolved matters instead of equating good relationships with universal agreement.

tabs.label: Choice
tabs.body: Declining an invitation can reflect workload, a poor prior experience, or a personal boundary. Do not infer resistance to equity. Keep appropriate updates available and examine the agency’s own missed responsibilities.

check.question: What sustains the relationship?
check.correct: A usable response, repair of missed promises, and a review of usefulness with participants.
check.feedbackCorrect: The review examines the agency’s responsibilities as well as participation.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Attendance alone does not show reciprocal engagement. Agreement-based ratings and repeated invitations without responses shift responsibility to partners. Examine delivery, give the overdue decision account, and respect a partner’s choice without labeling it as lack of commitment.

items.text: Explain the changed contact route.
Describe why a proposal remains unresolved.
Arrange the missed support through the person or area responsible.
Set a date for an overdue answer.
No criticism means trust is restored.
Declining an invitation means the partner resists equity.

options: Provide the overdue response, ask about missed commitments, and respect the choice.
Count the first event as complete engagement.
responses: The label ignores the agency’s own follow-through.
This restores accountability without demanding participation.
The relationship includes outcomes and responses, not only attendance.

move.failure: People give time and see neither influence nor accountability.
